{"docket_number": "53", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1968", "first_party": "Harold Kaufman ", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "United States", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit", "argued": ["1968-11-19T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Can a federal prisoner challenge unlawfully-seized evidence in a post-conviction proceeding?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

During his trial for armed robbery of a federally insured savings and loan association, Harold Kaufman admitted to the crime but unsuccessfully claimed insanity. He was convicted and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed. Kaufman then filed a post-conviction motion in district court challenging the evidence that proved his sanity. He alleged that the evidence was unlawfully seized in violation of the Fourth Amendment. The district court denied relief, holding that unlawful search and seizure was not an available attack in post-conviction proceedings. The Eighth Circuit affirmed.

", "conclusion": "

Yes. Justice William J. Brennan, writing for a 5-3 majority, reversed and remanded. The Supreme Court held that Kaufman could challenge unlawfully seized evidence in a post-conviction proceeding. There was no need to show special circumstances. The fact that Kaufman admitted to the crime was irrelevant because he claimed an affirmative defense.

Justice Hugo L. Black dissented, arguing that prisoners can only challenge evidence post-conviction in special circumstances. The prisoner should have to cast some shadow of doubt on his guilt. Justice John M. Harlan wrote a separate dissent, writing that Kaufman did not show special circumstances, so should not be allowed to challenge the evidence post conviction. Justice Potter Stewart joined in the dissent. Justice Thurgood Marshall did not participate.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll call the next case now. Number 53, Harold Kaufman, petitioner versus United States. Mr. Jacob. Yes, Your Honor. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. I'm Bruce Jacob and seated at the council table with me is Mr. William Skinner. We represent the petitioner, Harold Kaufman. Well, this case involves Section 2255 of the Federal Judicial Code, and the main issue in the case, we feel, is whether a federal inmate should be entitled to utilize Section 2255 to raise the question of whether or not he was convicted on the basis of illegally obtained evidence. At the present time, there is a conflict in the approaches taken by the various courts and the various federal circuits throughout the country. This case arose in the Eighth Circuit, which takes the very strict view that search and seizure issues cannot be raised by 2255. Ordinarily, they must be raised through direct appeal. Kaufman was tried in 1964 in the Eastern District of Missouri for the crime of robbery of a savings and loan association, a federal savings and loan. At the trial, he and his attorney conceded that Kaufman had been the man who had held up the savings and loan. The only issue it developed at the outset of the trial was whether or not he had been insane at the time. There was some evidence introduced, evidence which had been obtained from Kaufman's person and from the car which he had been driving at the time he was arrested. This evidence was introduced over the objection of counsel. During closing argument on the issue of insanity, the prosecutor referred to some of this evidence. Kaufman was convicted and sentenced to 20 years. He took a direct appeal to the Eighth Circuit, and a new attorney was appointed to represent him in that appeal. Kaufman claims, although the record doesn't bear this out, Kaufman claims in an affidavit which is included as an appendix to our brief, that he wrote to his newly appointed appellate attorney and asked that he raise all the constitutional issues which appeared in the trial record, including the issue of whether or not illegally obtained evidence had been used against him. The attorney, however, did not raise this issue in the appeal, in the briefs, or at the oral argument. Oral argument took place in March of 1965. In April, approximately a month and a half after oral argument, Kaufman, who was now at the Atlanta Penitentiary, wrote to the attorney, to his appellate attorney, and said, his letter, by the way, is included as an appendix to our brief, and said in substance that there's a point which has not been raised. There was an illegal search and seizure of my coat and of my car, and this evidence violates the rules or violated the rule of Preston v. United States. This is a constitutional question that should have been raised. Please see if you can't raise it at this time. The attorney, who also has submitted an affidavit, which is included as an appendix to our brief, went to the clerk of the Eighth Circuit and asked whether there was any way to raise the issue at that time after oral argument. The clerk advised him that there was no formal way of raising the issue at that time. The clerk suggested, however, that if the attorney would send him a copy, or send him the letter that Kaufman had sent to the attorney, that this letter would be forwarded to the panel of judges who had heard the case. And this, in fact, is what took place. The letter was forwarded to the clerk. The clerk forwarded it to the panel in June of 1965. The opinion of the Eighth Circuit was handed down in September 1965, and in the opinion there was no reference whatever to the search and seizure issue. The opinion was completely silent on this issue. Kaufman then took certiorari to this court, and the same attorney who had represented him in the appeal filed the petition for certiorari. And one of the issues raised in that petition for certiorari was the issue of whether or not illegally seized evidence had been used against Kaufman at his trial. And in the petition for certiorari, and the legal argument included in that petition, the appellate attorney pointed out that he had attempted to raise this issue informally by letter, but that the Eighth Circuit had been silent on this issue in its opinion. Well, certiorari was denied. And then in 1966, Kaufman filed a motion to vacate under Section 2255 with the Eastern District, in the Eastern District of Missouri. Another attorney was appointed to represent him. A supplemental motion to vacate was filed. And in the supplemental motion, the issue was raised, the issue of whether or not evidence illegally obtained from his car had been improperly used against him at his trial. An evidentiary hearing was held before the same judge, the same judge who had presided at the trial. In March 1967, an order was entered by the trial judge denying relief on all the issues presented by the motion to vacate. And in the 12-page order, only one paragraph was devoted to the search and seizure issue. And this is what the court said. This is found in the appendix on page 21. One, the record does not, he said, one of the issues is the issue of whether or not illegally seized evidence was used against Kaufman. Quote, the record does not substantiate the search and seizure claim. In any event, the matter was not assigned as error on Kaufman's appeal from conviction and is not available as a ground for collateral attack in the instant Section 2255 motion. And the judge then cited cases of the Eighth Circuit, which take the very strict view that search and seizure issues should be raised by direct appeal, not through collateral attack under Section 2255. The trial judge then denied Kaufman leave to appeal in forma pauperis from this ruling. Kaufman filed a motion for leave to proceed to appeal in forma pauperis in the appellate court. That court likewise denied the motion and certiorari has been taken from that ruling. The narrow issue, the very narrow issue before this court then is whether the Eighth Circuit properly denied Kaufman's motion for leave to appeal in forma pauperis. But I believe that in order to answer that question, we must answer several other questions, one of which is whether the strict rule of law applied by the District Judge, the strict rule of law applied by the Eighth Circuit to the effect that search and seizure issues cannot be raised through Section 2255, was a proper rule of law. As I said earlier, there is a conflict among the Federal Circuits. Did they hold that so-called absolute rule that never could be raised through 2255 or that the strict rule of law applied by the Eighth Circuit that I have discovered all indicate that it's an absolute rule. They say that this is to be raised by direct appeal, not by 2255. There are no cases that I know of in which the Eighth Circuit has allowed it to be raised in the first instance through 2255. There are a number of circuits which follow this strict view. The District of Columbia has taken a more liberal approach in the Thornton case, Thornton v. United States. In that decision, the District of Columbia Court of Appeals stated that they would at least consider a motion to vacate under Section 2255, which raises a search and seizure claim, but they would be very strict about granting relief. They would only grant relief where exceptional circumstances are present, but they will at least consider the question. The Fourth Circuit and the Tenth Circuit have taken a very liberal approach in the Gaetan case and in the Sutton case of the Fourth Circuit. There they have said through dicta, that's not part of the holding of these decisions, but they have indicated that since MAP v. Ohio at least, search and seizure claims under the Fourth Amendment have a constitutional basis, and therefore these claims should be allowed to be raised by 2255, just as any other constitutional claim. When 2255 was adopted back in 1948, the purpose of the statute was not to narrow the constitutional right to habeas corpus. The purpose was not to limit or narrow the remedy which had previously been available to a federal inmate through habeas corpus. The only purpose was to simplify the mechanics involved in obtaining collateral relief. The purpose was to adopt some of the simple mechanics which are available through corum nobis. In other words, the motion or the petition was to be filed in the trial court rather than the court which is located in the district in which you were incarcerated. This was more convenient because the trial court has all the records and files in the case, and this means the prisoner will not have to be conveyed back to the... Well, this is more convenient because the trial court has all the records, and 2255 distributes the load of these collateral motions throughout the country. Prior to 1948, the bulk of these petitions for habeas corpus by federal prisoners were being filed in districts in which federal prisons were located. But the remedy cannot be any narrower than the constitutional remedy of habeas corpus. In fact, this court has said so in cases such as the Heyman case and Sanders v. U.S. In fact, if 2255 is construed to be any narrower than constitutional habeas corpus or statutory habeas corpus under Section 2241, there would be grave questions as to the constitutionality of Section 2255. So we take the position that the rule of the Eighth Circuit is improper, that a federal inmate filing a petition or a motion to vacate under 2255 should be entitled to the same relief that a state inmate is entitled to through habeas corpus. There are numerous cases which have held that a state inmate can use federal habeas corpus to raise search and seizure claims. The Solicitor General's Office has argued that there may be some policy reasons for providing a different treatment for federal inmates. There may be some policy reasons for allowing a state inmate to raise search and seizure issues through habeas corpus while not allowing a federal inmate to raise similar issues under 2255. But, as Justice Scali-Wright pointed out in his dissenting opinion in the Thornton case, there are many instances in which a federal inmate may not even get one judicial review of his search and seizure claims if he is not allowed to utilize the remedy of 2255. Because in many cases, the issue is not even raised at the trial level. Suppose a federal inmate pleads guilty. He's induced to plead guilty by the fact that the FBI have a great deal of illegally seized evidence against him. He doesn't realize that the evidence was illegally seized. There's nothing in the record to indicate that his plea of guilty was induced by illegally seized evidence. The only way you can get at this issue is to hold a hearing under 2255 and allow evidence to be developed on this issue. Or if an attorney fails to file a motion to suppress evidence and fails to object to evidence at the trial. In a case such as this, there is nothing in the trial record to indicate that the defendant had some valid search and seizure issues. And there is nothing to be reviewed on direct appeal. The only way you can review the question of whether or not his attorney adequately represented him, and the only way you can get at this question of whether the failure to raise this issue, the denial of constitutional rights, is through 2255. So we submit that the... Are you arguing, Mr. Jacobs, that the 2255 Court must consider every constitutional claim, even though it might have been raised on appeal, or only that it shall be discretionary with the 2255 Court whether or not to hear it? It should be discretionary in this sense, Your Honor, that if an inmate has raised the issue fully at his trial, has had a full appeal on the issue, I believe the 2255 Court should at least look at this, but I don't think the 2255 Court in the case such as that would require a specific question. I don't think in the case of a state prisoner, he's entitled to have every constitutional claim that he might have made a ground of appeal in the state courts. Well, it's true, gentlemen. It's entertained by the federal habeas court, is it? I mean, that's still a matter of discretion, isn't it, with the federal habeas court? Well, I think you're right, that it would be a matter of discretion, in that collateral relief... There may be a rather limited discretion in many of these cases, but nevertheless, there is... Federal relief cannot be used in the same way as an appeal is used, and you can only raise exceptional questions through habeas corpus or 2255. It has to be a very serious violation of these constitutional rights before the trial court should be required to consider it. Will it raise? Yes, it's anonymous.
